articles.title: FIVE YEARS LATER, A COURT SUMMONS: Rochdale residents report historic Council Tax demands as arrears reach £28.4m
articles.excerpt: Several residents tell Rochdale Daily they have received summonses for old Council Tax bills, including a 2021 account. With arrears reportedly £28.4m, we examine recovery rules, compare council finances, and list free debt help.
articles.content_html:
ROCHDALE DAILY INVESTIGATION | 12 OCTOBER 2026

Several residents have approached Rochdale Daily reporting that they have received court summonses over Council Tax bills from previous years. One account relates to a bill dating back to 2021 — approximately five years ago. These reports are residents' accounts; the paper has not independently examined the full Council Tax and court history for every case.

For households already struggling with essentials, an old demand coupled with court costs can create significant additional pressure. The issue raises questions about whether Rochdale Council has changed its approach to historic arrears, what notices were originally sent, how payments are allocated and what support is offered before enforcement.

ROCHDALE'S £28.4 MILLION COUNCIL TAX ARREARS

Government collection returns for 2025/26, as compiled by Council Tax Helpline, place Rochdale's total Council Tax arrears outstanding at around £28.4 million at 31 March 2026, including recovery-related costs — up approximately 12.7% over the year. This is not the amount owed by any individual and should not be divided among residents as if everybody owes it.

Rochdale Council's draft 2025/26 accounts use a different accounting measure. Their Council Tax debtor balance increased from £19.585 million at 31 March 2025 to £21.958 million at 31 March 2026. Those figures should not be added to the £28.4 million or treated as directly interchangeable; they reflect different financial reporting definitions.

Sources: government 2025/26 collection returns https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/collection-rates-for-council-tax-and-non-domestic-rates-in-england-2025-to-2026; authority comparison https://www.counciltaxhelpline.co.uk/research/council-tax-arrears/; council draft accounts, Note 15 https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s122950/Append.%201%20for%20Draft%20Statement%20of%20Accounts%20202526.pdf

CAN THE COUNCIL SUMMON SOMEONE FOR A 2021 BILL IN 2026?

Potentially, yes. Regulation 34(3) of the Council Tax (Administration and Enforcement) Regulations 1992 generally gives a council six years from the date the sum became due to bring proceedings for a liability order. A bill described as relating to 2021 is not automatically outside that period in October 2026; the precise demand and due dates matter.

A previously granted liability order changes the position, because subsequent enforcement is not necessarily subject to the same six-year limit for starting the original proceedings. Anyone disputing liability or the timetable needs their account history, copies of notices, and dates of any earlier court orders.

Source: Council Tax (Administration and Enforcement) Regulations 1992, Regulation 34 https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/1992/613/regulation/34

WHAT ARE THE COURT COSTS — AND WHAT SHOULD YOU DO?

Rochdale Council's court-hearings guidance says a summons may carry court costs of £101.50 or £102. If the council obtains a liability order, enforcement fees may increase what someone has to pay. A summons is not proof that the amount claimed is accurate: residents can challenge liability or payment records through the proper process.

Residents should NOT ignore a summons. Ask immediately for the annual bill, statutory reminders, itemised transactions and credits, discounts and exemptions, dates notices were sent, and confirmation of whether a liability order already exists. If challenging liability before magistrates, follow the court-hearing telephone attendance instructions on Rochdale Council's website and the summons itself. Financial hardship alone is not normally a defence to liability, but it is a reason to seek an affordable arrangement and specialist debt advice without delay.

Source: Rochdale Council court-hearing guidance https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/council-tax/problems-paying-council-tax/3; contact Council Tax 0300 303 8870 or council.tax@rochdale.gov.uk

COULD PAYMENTS BE GOING TO DIFFERENT TAX YEARS?

Rochdale Council explains that its software normally allocates a payment matching a current-year instalment to the current year. A payment matching more than one such instalment can also be allocated to the current balance rather than old arrears. Other payments may go to the oldest debt. Residents seeking to pay arrears for a specific year are advised to tell the council explicitly which year's debt the payment is intended to reduce.

That does not establish an error in any resident's case, but it makes a full payment allocation history essential when a debt resurfaces years later.

Source: Rochdale Council, 'How payments are allocated' https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/council-tax/pay-council-tax

IS THIS A NEW HISTORIC-DEBT CRACKDOWN?

The public records do not prove that. The council was collecting older arrears before 2026. In October 2023 it reported collecting approximately £2.5 million in Council Tax arrears by the end of that August, about £400,000 more than in the comparable prior period.

To establish whether residents are receiving more summonses for old debts now, Rochdale Daily is seeking year-by-year summons figures broken down by the year of original liability, amounts claimed, recovery costs, cancelled summonses and changes in recovery policy. We have not found such a breakdown in publicly accessible reporting.

Source: Council meeting reports, October 2023 https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/documents/g6401/Public%20reports%20pack%2018th-Oct-2023%2018.00%20Council.pdf?T=10

AND WHAT ABOUT THE £50 MILLION UPPERBANKS LOANS?

Rochdale Council's draft accounts show £50.309 million in contractual loans owing from council-owned companies associated with the Upperbanks hotel and residential development at 31 March 2026. During 2025/26 the loans accrued approximately £2.020 million in interest and recorded £132,000 in repayments. Their loan arrangements include payment holidays and other contractual conditions.

These are NOT unpaid household taxes and the size of a commercial loan balance does not, by itself, imply it is overdue or in default. Crucially, no evidence has been established connecting Upperbanks lending with the pursuit of old Council Tax bills. The legitimate point of comparison is whether the council makes its debt-management decisions transparent across both areas of public finance.

Source: Rochdale Council draft 2025/26 accounts, loan disclosure https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s122950/Append.%201%20for%20Draft%20Statement%20of%20Accounts%20202526.pdf

FREE HELP IF YOU CANNOT AFFORD YOUR COUNCIL TAX

StepChange Debt Charity: 0800 138 1111, free advice online at https://www.stepchange.org. Advisers can help prioritise Council Tax arrears, assess household finances, work with creditors and consider suitable debt solutions.

National Debtline: 0808 808 4000, https://nationaldebtline.org. Independent help with Council Tax, summonses, liability orders, enforcement agents and budgeting.

Citizens Advice Rochdale: 0808 278 7803. Rochdale advice sessions include Number One Riverside, Smith Street. Check current drop-in and outreach arrangements at https://www.citizensadvicesort.org.uk/offices/rochdale. Support includes benefits, housing, debt and practical assistance.

MoneyHelper: find free regulated debt advice and budgeting guidance at https://www.moneyhelper.org.uk/en/money-troubles/dealing-with-debt/debt-advice-locator.

Rochdale Council Tax team: 0300 303 8870, council.tax@rochdale.gov.uk, https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/council-tax. Request an itemised statement, challenge inaccurate liability through the prescribed route, discuss affordable payment arrangements and ask about Council Tax Support.

COUNCIL TAX REDUCTIONS AND EMERGENCY SUPPORT

Rochdale residents on low incomes may qualify for Council Tax Support. Single-person discounts, disability-related reductions and statutory exemptions can apply where conditions are met. The council also has a discretionary Council Tax discount policy under Section 13A of the Local Government Finance Act 1992 for certain exceptional circumstances. Ask the Revenues and Benefits team what evidence is required.

Source: Rochdale Council discretionary Council Tax policy, updated March 2026 https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/directory-record/2426/discretionary-council-tax-discount-policy; Council Tax services https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/council-tax

Rochdale's Crisis and Resilience Fund supports eligible residents facing financial emergencies, including certain emergency payments, housing assistance and essential items. It does not automatically settle Council Tax arrears, but may relieve pressure on everyday essentials. Cost of Living Services: 01706 923685. Details at https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/cost-living/crisis-resilience-fund.

Some people can obtain a 'Breathing Space' debt respite through an authorised debt adviser. Standard Breathing Space can provide up to 60 days' protection from most enforcement action and interest or charges on qualifying debts, subject to eligibility. A separate scheme exists for qualifying mental health crisis treatment. It does not write off debts. Government guidance: https://www.gov.uk/options-for-dealing-with-your-debts/breathing-space.

SIX QUESTIONS FOR ROCHDALE COUNCIL

1. How many summonses issued in 2025 and 2026 related to Council Tax liabilities originating in 2021 or earlier?

2. Has any targeted exercise or policy change been introduced to recover older Council Tax debts, and when?

3. How much has been added to old balances through court and enforcement costs, and how much was actually collected?

4. How many summonses have been withdrawn because of incorrect liability, missing payment credits, defective notices or limitation issues?

5. What safeguards are used where residents disclose disability, serious illness, unemployment or acute financial hardship?

6. How many residents received repayment arrangements, Council Tax Support or exceptional discounts before enforcement progressed?

Rochdale Daily invites Rochdale Borough Council to respond with records and explanations. The paper also invites residents to share experiences of historic summonses confidentially at news@rochdaledaily.co.uk. Do not send personal financial reference numbers or identifiable court documents publicly; redact sensitive information before sharing.

THE BOTTOM LINE

Council Tax is a lawful obligation, and the council can pursue valid arrears. Residents are equally entitled to a clear statement of what they owe, when it became payable, which notices were served, how every payment was credited and what help is available if they cannot pay.

Rising arrears are documented. A new campaign of historic summonses, or a connection to Upperbanks, has not yet been demonstrated. Obtaining the age breakdown of court cases is the next test of the accounts residents have brought to Rochdale Daily.

General information only; individual debt cases require prompt, tailored advice and attention to any court deadline.

articles.title: Ten years without answers: the continuing search for Rochdale’s Jack Stewart
articles.excerpt: Jack Stewart vanished from Spotland on 8 February 2016. His missing-person appeal remains listed a decade later. Here are the original clothing details, what the community did, and how to report information safely.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Daily | Missing persons appeal | 12 October 2026

Ten years after Jack Stewart disappeared from Spotland, a national missing-person charity continues to carry his photograph and an appeal for information. Jack was last reported seen at about 8am on Monday 8 February 2016, at his home on Ings Lane in Rochdale. What happened next remains unknown in the public appeal. For anyone who remembers that morning, or who notices something potentially significant while walking in the area, information can still be passed directly to the police.

Jack's appeal is currently listed by the independent charity Missing People, with reference 16-000774. The charity records him as 68 when he went missing; some original police reporting described him as 69. The important details are the date, location and identifying information, rather than trying to resolve that inconsistency without original records.

Official Missing People appeal: https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/help-us-find/jack-stewart-16-000774

THE MORNING JACK WAS LAST SEEN

At around 8am on Monday 8 February 2016, Jack was seen at his home on Ings Lane, Spotland. Police said his disappearance was extremely out of character, noting that he liked routine in his life. That detail matters because those familiar with his everyday movements may be able to distinguish an ordinary journey from a change in habit. The information available publicly does not establish which direction he travelled, what happened after 8am or why he disappeared.

Contemporary reports describe Jack as a white man, approximately 5ft 9in tall, with brown-and-grey hair worn in a distinctive 'teddy boy' style. His clothing was described in early coverage as a BLACK QUILTED JACKET, BLACK JEANS, STRIPED SOCKS and a DARK-COLOURED CHECK SHIRT. These are the last publicly reported clothing details, not proof that any item would remain recognisable today. Colours, fabrics and descriptions may change over time. The police are best placed to assess the significance of any discovery.

Sources: original 2016 Greater Manchester Police appeal, reproduced in subsequent MEN coverage https://www.manchestereveningnews.co.uk/news/greater-manchester-news/police-new-appeal-over-missing-10871344; later account with clothing description https://www.inkl.com/news/the-men-women-and-children-missing-from-home-this-christmas; charity appeal https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/help-us-find/jack-stewart-16-000774

HOW ROCHDALE RESPONDED

Local people helped to look for Jack soon after he disappeared. Later reporting records that around 60 members of the public joined a search organised from Brotherod Community Centre, near his home. The response reflected a community unwilling to let a neighbour vanish without notice. Those efforts did not produce a publicly confirmed resolution in the records reviewed for this report.

Source: Manchester Evening News coverage of historic missing Greater Manchester residents https://www.inkl.com/news/the-men-women-and-children-missing-from-home-this-christmas

JACK AS A PERSON, NOT JUST A MISSING PERSON

Jack was known to police as someone who valued routine. That is one small glimpse of the life behind the appeal: a man whose ordinary day was sufficiently familiar that his absence immediately stood out. Rochdale Daily has not been able to verify specific hobbies, employment history, or details about a wife, partner, children or surviving relatives from reliable public sources. We will not speculate about them or print supposed family memories without permission.

Anyone close to Jack who wishes to share family-approved memories of his interests, favourite places, the things that made him laugh or his daily routine may contact the newsroom. There is no expectation that relatives should speak publicly. Their privacy and wellbeing come first, and the missing-person appeal does not require the family to relive events for others' curiosity.

TEN YEARS ON: NO CONCLUSIONS WITHOUT EVIDENCE

Jack's continued listing on Missing People means the public appeal has not been withdrawn on the charity's site at the time of this report. It does not establish that he died, that he was harmed by another person, or that the police are pursuing any particular theory. The precise investigative status, searches undertaken since 2016 and any new leads have not been confirmed in a current statement from Greater Manchester Police.

A decade passing does not turn an unverified theory into fact. Whether someone remembers a sighting, has a dated photograph or recalls an unusual circumstance, even a detail that seemed insignificant at the time may be worth submitting to the officers responsible.

IF YOU ARE WALKING YOUR DOG AND FIND SOMETHING CONCERNING

If you come across clothing, personal effects, bones or other material that might be connected to a missing-person case, DO NOT try to decide yourself whether it belongs to Jack. Many items will have entirely unrelated explanations.

If you suspect you have found human remains or a scene requiring an urgent police response, call 999. Do not touch, move, uncover, collect or take anything home; do not dig or disturb the surrounding ground. Keep children and dogs away and avoid walking through the immediate area. Move to a safe position, note the location using a nearby landmark or phone map pin if it is safe to do so, and wait for police instructions.

For a non-urgent recollection, possible sighting or information about the 2016 disappearance, contact Greater Manchester Police on 101 or via https://www.gmp.police.uk. Tell the operator this concerns Jack Stewart, missing from Spotland on 8 February 2016, and provide the Missing People reference 16-000774 as an identifying aid. A charity reference is not necessarily a police incident number.

Please do not post photographs of potentially sensitive evidence, suspected remains, or unverified names online. Do not organise an unsupervised search of private land, woodland or waterways. Any possible discovery should go straight to police, who can preserve and assess evidence and contact families appropriately.

General official guidance on missing-person sightings and reporting: https://www.gov.uk/report-missing-person; UK Missing Persons Unit: https://www.nationalcrimeagency.gov.uk/missingpersons

WHAT IF YOU SIMPLY REMEMBER SOMETHING?

People who lived or worked around Ings Lane, Spotland or neighbouring areas in February 2016 might remember a morning journey, conversation or circumstance that they never associated with the disappearance. You do not need to be certain that a memory is significant before discussing it with police. Explain how confident you are, distinguish what you personally saw from what someone else told you, and do not guess to fill gaps.

The charity Missing People also accepts information confidentially. Call or text 116 000, or use the 'Report a sighting' link at https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/help-us-find/jack-stewart-16-000774. Contacting the charity should not delay a call to police where there is an immediate danger or potential crime scene.

HELP FOR FAMILIES, FRIENDS AND ANYONE AFFECTED

The experience of an unresolved disappearance can affect loved ones and entire communities for years. Missing People offers free, confidential practical and emotional support to relatives, friends and people who are missing themselves. Call or text 116 000. Its family support team can also be reached at family.support@missingpeople.org.uk. Its helpline website lists current operating hours.

Missing People family help: https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/get-help/help-services/family-support; helpline: https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/get-help/helpline. If you are distressed by something you have encountered, the police or an appropriate health professional can advise on immediate support; Samaritans offers someone to talk to at any hour on 116 123.

ANY INFORMATION MAY MATTER

Jack Stewart was last seen in Rochdale on 8 February 2016. The clothing described in early appeals — a black quilted jacket, black jeans, striped socks and a dark check shirt — remains a potentially useful historical reference, but identification is the responsibility of trained police and forensic professionals.

For his loved ones, what matters is not speculation but a reliable answer. Ten years later, anyone with real information can still help by passing it to the right people. Rochdale Daily invites Greater Manchester Police and Jack's family, if they wish, to provide any verified updated details for a correction or follow-up; no family member is being asked to take part publicly.

Sources: https://www.missingpeople.org.uk/help-us-find/jack-stewart-16-000774; https://www.inkl.com/news/the-men-women-and-children-missing-from-home-this-christmas; https://www.gov.uk/report-missing-person

Hobbies and family composition have not been independently verified. Potential evidence should be reported directly to police without being disturbed.

articles.title: 651 SEWAGE SPILLS INTO THE RIVER ROCH: 3,271 HOURS OF DISCHARGES — WHAT IS IN OUR WATER AND WHO PAYS?
articles.excerpt: Seventeen outlets discharged into the River Roch in 2025. Rochdale Daily examines what residents and wildlife may be exposed to, how water is tested, why storm overflows operate, and which fines have actually been imposed.
articles.content_html:
ROCHDALE DAILY INVESTIGATION | 12 OCTOBER 2026

The River Roch received 651 recorded storm-overflow discharges during 2025, lasting a combined 3,271 hours across 17 outlets, according to the environmental data project Top of the Poops, drawing on water-company returns submitted to the Environment Agency. Two further outlets listed in the same river table reported no discharges. Every identified operator was United Utilities.

The numbers are startling, but require careful interpretation. The 3,271 hours are added together across outlets; some will have run simultaneously. It does not mean the whole river was continuously receiving discharges for 3,271 hours. Neither the duration monitors nor the count establish the volume released, chemical or bacterial concentrations, any particular person's illness, or whether an individual discharge was unlawful.

Sources: Top of the Poops, River Roch 2025 monitoring summary, https://www.top-of-the-poops.org/waterway/united-utilities/river-roch; Environment Agency, 2025 national storm overflow annual returns, https://www.data.gov.uk/dataset/19f6064d-7356-466f-844e-d20ea10ae9fd/event-duration-monitoring-storm-overflows-annual-returns

WHERE DID THE SEWAGE ENTER?

Rochdale wastewater treatment works recorded 104 spills lasting approximately 1,503 hours — around 46% of the 3,271 combined hours. Oakenrod combined sewer overflow recorded 87 events lasting approximately 508 hours. At Heywood (Botany) treatment works the figures were 35 events and 240 hours; Sudden Valley sewer recorded 83 events and 235 hours.

Other identified outlets included Smith Bridge Road (20 events, 158 hours), Hooley Bridge (39, 140), Albert Royds Street (73, 138), Peel Lane No. 1 (43, 92) and Peel Lane No. 2 (35, 69). These outlets are along different stretches of the river and should not all be described as being in the town centre.

Figures: https://www.top-of-the-poops.org/waterway/united-utilities/river-roch

WHY DOES THIS HAPPEN? MOST ARE NOT BURST PIPES

Much of the North West uses combined sewers, carrying rainwater from roofs and roads in the same pipes as foul sewage from toilets, bathrooms and businesses. During heavy rainfall or snowmelt, the combined flow can exceed sewer and treatment capacity. Storm overflows act as designed pressure-release points, allowing diluted, often untreated sewage and rainwater into rivers rather than letting the system back up into homes. At treatment works, storm tanks store surplus flows, but may overflow when capacity is exceeded.

That explains how the infrastructure is intended to work; it does not establish that all 651 individual River Roch operations were authorised. Legal discharge depends on the actual permit, flow thresholds and conditions at the time. Equipment failure, maintenance problems, insufficient capacity or inappropriate operation can also lead to pollution breaches. It would take rainfall, flow-to-full-treatment, maintenance and permit records to determine the reason and legality of each event.

United Utilities has said that 54% of its North West sewerage network is combined, and describes plans for further capacity and rainwater separation. The Environment Agency says longstanding underinvestment and poor asset maintenance contribute to high national overflow usage. These are wider explanations, not documented causes assigned individually to each River Roch spill.

Sources: Environment Agency, what storm overflow monitors show, https://www.gov.uk/government/news/fewer-and-shorter-storm-overflow-spills-in-2025-new-monitoring-data-shows; United Utilities better rivers report, https://www.unitedutilities.com/globalassets/documents/pdf/united-utilities-better-rivers-report-2024.pdf; Environment Agency explanation, https://environmentagency.blog.gov.uk/2025/03/27/what-are-the-2024-edm-annual-returns/

WHAT DOES 'MEASURING WATER QUALITY' ACTUALLY MEAN?

Event Duration Monitors (EDMs) measure WHEN an overflow runs and HOW LONG it runs; they do not measure the litres discharged, how much faecal bacteria is present, the ammonia concentration, or whether water is safe for people to enter. National spill counts use the regulatory event-counting methodology, rather than equalling every individual sensor activation.

River health is assessed separately through Environment Agency sampling, ecological surveys and modelling. Measurements can include dissolved oxygen, ammonia, phosphate, biological oxygen demand, temperature, acidity (pH) and selected chemical contaminants. Ecologists also survey fish, invertebrates and water plants, and consider habitat modification. An overall ecological classification combines several measures, so improvement in one chemical does not automatically mean the whole river is healthy.

For designated bathing waters, officials specifically test E. coli and intestinal enterococci as indicators of faecal contamination. Ordinary rivers are not necessarily sampled for those bacteria as regular bathing-water sites. No verified River Roch-wide 2025 bacteria sampling series has been identified in the sources examined. An overflow monitor cannot be used as a certificate of safe swimming water.

Sources: Environment Agency, river classification framework, https://engageenvironmentagency.uk.engagementhq.com/understanding-englands-water-environment/widgets/155553/faqs; Environment Agency, bathing-water bacteria testing, https://environmentagency.blog.gov.uk/2025/05/15/how-the-environment-agency-monitors-and-tests-bathing-water-quality/

WHAT DO THE RIVER'S ACTUAL TESTS SHOW?

There is documented progress as well as continuing concern. In August 2026 the Environment Agency reported that phosphate quality on the River Roch (Spodden to Irwell) improved from POOR in 2019 to GOOD in the 2025 classification. It attributed the improvement to treatment upgrades and a catchment-wide permitting system requiring better phosphorus removal at wastewater treatment works. That is an important environmental gain.

However, the Environment Agency's catchment records classify the lower Roch waterbody's ecological status as MODERATE in its published records: invertebrates were moderate and aquatic macrophytes (larger water plants) poor in the 2022 assessment. The source-to-Spodden waterbody also had moderate ecological status in the recorded classification. These classifications describe river condition, not evidence that the 2025 overflows caused each shortcoming. Historical chemical failures include persistent contaminants with multiple potential sources.

Sources: Environment Agency, August 2026 reporting, https://www.gov.uk/government/news/new-data-to-drive-action-to-improve-englands-rivers-and-lakes; Environment Agency lower River Roch waterbody, https://environment.data.gov.uk/catchment-planning/WaterBody/GB112069064600; upper River Roch waterbody, https://environment.data.gov.uk/catchment-planning/WaterBody/GB112069064720

HOW MIGHT PEOPLE AND PETS BE AFFECTED?

Untreated sewage-contaminated water can contain bacteria, viruses and parasites. Exposure while swimming, paddling, retrieving a ball or handling contaminated riverbank material can increase the risk of stomach illness, skin, eye or ear infection and, in some circumstances, severe infections. Risks depend on the actual organisms and concentration, exposure route and the person involved. The monitoring totals do not show that residents of Rochdale have been made ill by any specific spill.

Children and dog walkers using the riverbank should not mistake clear-looking water or a 'not currently spilling' monitor for proof of safety. Avoid swallowing untreated river water, wash hands after contact, keep pets from drinking discoloured or foul-smelling water, and keep children away from visible sewage contamination. Contact with the river is a different issue from the quality of treated drinking water delivered to household taps: these overflow figures do NOT show that Rochdale's tap water is contaminated.

Source: UKHSA/Environment Agency open-water health guidance, https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/swim-healthy-leaflet/swim-healthy

WHAT HAPPENS TO FISH, INSECTS AND WILDLIFE?

Sewage carries organic matter and nutrients. As microorganisms break down the waste, dissolved oxygen can fall, stressing fish and aquatic insects. Ammonia can be directly toxic to fish and invertebrates at sufficiently high concentrations; excessive nutrients can encourage algal growth and alter plant communities. Repeated pulses can affect sensitive species even where a river looks normal between storms.

The River Roch's invertebrate and plant classifications warrant continued scrutiny, but attribution matters: modified channels, urban runoff, other pollution and long-lived chemicals also affect ecological health. This investigation found no verified evidence that 651 measured overflow events killed a specified number of fish or animals in the Roch in 2025. The proper test would combine event timing with upstream/downstream sampling and evidence of wildlife impacts.

Source: Environment Agency evidence of ammonia and fish mortality in a separate investigated river pollution case, https://www.gov.uk/government/news/anglian-water-fined-300-000-after-pollution-killed-5-000-fish; River Roch classification, https://environment.data.gov.uk/catchment-planning/WaterBody/GB112069064600

IS THE RIVER GETTING BETTER?

At Rochdale wastewater treatment works, recorded overflow events fell from 116 in 2024 to 104 in 2025; discharge hours fell from approximately 1,679 to 1,503. Oakenrod likewise fell from 101 spills and around 662 hours in 2024 to 87 spills and around 508 hours in 2025. These are improvements in recorded overflow frequency and duration at those sites — NOT proof that concentrations of pathogens or total sewage volumes fell by the same proportions.

Across England, storm-overflow events fell by 35% and monitored spill duration fell by 48% in 2025 compared with 2024. The Environment Agency emphasises that 2025 was unusually dry, so these comparisons cannot all be attributed to improved infrastructure.

Sources: Rochdale works historical spill data, https://sewagemap.org.uk/locations/rochdale-wwtw; Oakenrod historical spill data, https://sewagemap.org.uk/locations/oakenrod-cso; Environment Agency national 2025 figures, https://www.gov.uk/government/news/fewer-and-shorter-storm-overflow-spills-in-2025-new-monitoring-data-shows

IS UNITED UTILITIES FINED FOR SEWAGE DISCHARGES?

Yes, when regulators establish breaches. The Environment Agency can investigate permit breaches and prosecute serious offences. Courts determine criminal fines, while other cases may be resolved through environmental enforcement undertakings and restoration payments. But discharging from a permitted storm overflow during qualifying conditions is not automatically a criminal offence, and a published spill count is NOT a count of proved illegal discharges.

On 8 September 2026 United Utilities was fined £900,000, plus £62,225 prosecution costs and a £2,000 surcharge, after admitting five environmental permit offences over sewage discharges on the FYLDE COAST following a pipe failure in 2023. In a separate case, United Utilities agreed a £517,000 environmental enforcement undertaking following permit breaches affecting the RIVER TAME in Tameside. Neither was a fine for these 651 River Roch events.

Ofwat opened an enforcement case into United Utilities' wider wastewater operations in July 2024. As of the regulator's latest published investigation-status page, that case remains OPEN; opening a case is not a finding that particular River Roch spills were illegal.

Crucially, Rochdale Daily has not identified a published fine or formal penalty specifically attributable to the 651 River Roch discharges in 2025. That is NOT a finding that no breaches occurred: the Environment Agency must be asked for inspection, incident and enforcement records for each relevant permit.

Sources: Environment Agency Fylde conviction, https://www.gov.uk/government/news/water-company-fined-record-900k-after-coastline-sewage-spill; River Tame payment, https://www.gov.uk/government/news/environment-agency-secures500k-for-tame-catchment-improvements; Ofwat enforcement status, https://www.ofwat.gov.uk/investigation-into-sewage-treatment-works-and-networks/

WHEN WILL IT STOP?

United Utilities says it plans to invest more than £3 billion in storm-overflow improvements across the North West, targeting a 60% reduction in spills over the decade to 2030. In December 2025 it also announced a £4.5 million storage project at CASTLETON treatment works, expected to complete by the end of 2026 — but that scheme concerns Trub Brook and the River Irk, NOT the River Roch outlets in the 651 tally.

For meaningful local accountability, United Utilities should provide a dated, outlet-by-outlet plan for Rochdale wastewater treatment works, Oakenrod, Sudden Valley and the other River Roch overflows, with construction milestones, budgets, expected reductions and results after completion.

Sources: United Utilities investment strategy, https://corporate.unitedutilities.com/better-rivers/; Castleton project announcement, https://www.unitedutilities.com/corporate/newsroom/latest-news/united-utilities-starts-4.5m-scheme-in-castleton/

QUESTIONS FOR UNITED UTILITIES AND THE ENVIRONMENT AGENCY

Rochdale Daily is asking: (1) Of the 651 recorded River Roch events in 2025, how many were checked against rainfall and permit limits, and were any found to be unauthorised? (2) What were the estimated discharge volumes and upstream/downstream E. coli, enterococci, ammonia and dissolved-oxygen measurements near Rochdale works and Oakenrod? (3) What fish kills, wildlife incidents or public health complaints have been linked by regulators to the relevant outlets? (4) Which sites were inspected and what warnings, civil penalties, enforcement undertakings or prosecutions resulted? (5) Exactly which River Roch upgrades have been funded, when will they be completed and how will the effect be measured?

Residents witnessing suspected sewage or dead fish can report water pollution to the Environment Agency's 24-hour hotline, 0800 80 70 60, or its online report-water-pollution service. Note the date, location, smell, colour and any visible debris; do not enter dangerous water to gather evidence.

Source: https://www.gov.uk/report-water-pollution

THE BOTTOM LINE

Six hundred and fifty-one recorded sewage discharges are an important indicator of pressure on the River Roch's sewerage system, not 651 proven crimes. There is measurable progress in phosphate and at some monitored sites; there is also a compelling need for bacteriological data, permit compliance evidence and outlet-level investment results. Residents deserve those answers before being told the river is either safe or beyond recovery.

Right of reply: United Utilities and the Environment Agency can submit any updated data, a statement, permit documents, monitoring results or corrections to news@rochdaledaily.co.uk.

articles.title: BREAKING INVESTIGATION: £50.3m owed by Rochdale Council companies as £19.5m Council Tax shortfall raises scrutiny
articles.excerpt: Rochdale's draft accounts show £50.309m in Upperbanks company loan balances, £2.02m interest added and only £132,000 repaid in 2025/26. We examine the figures, the 2022 decisions and the councillors responsible for oversight.
articles.content_html:
BREAKING INVESTIGATION | ROCHDALE DAILY

Rochdale Borough Council's own draft accounts reveal that three companies behind the Upperbanks development owed it £50.309 million in contractual loans at 31 March 2026. In the preceding financial year, just £132,000 was repaid while £2.020 million in interest accrued, increasing the total balance from £48.262 million.

The figures sit alongside reporting that the borough accumulated a £19.5 million Council Tax collection shortfall over the decade since 2016. These are very different forms of money: Council Tax is revenue for services, while Upperbanks loans finance long-term property assets and are not necessarily due for repayment now. Yet both invite scrutiny of how the authority manages public finances.

Source: Rochdale Borough Council, draft Statement of Accounts 2025/26, note on soft loans, printed page 81: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/downloads/file/3217/2025-2026-statement-of-accounts-draft-

Source: Roch Valley Radio, 'Council tax shortfall in Rochdale of almost £20m in 10 years', 12 June 2026: https://www.rochvalleyradio.com/news/local-news/council-tax-shortfall-in-rochdale-of-almost-20m-in-10-years/

WHAT IS UPPERBANKS AND HOW MUCH IS OWED?

The £60 million Upperbanks scheme, beside Rochdale Riverside, comprises 242 rental apartments and a 146-room Hampton by Hilton hotel. The development received more than £17 million from the Future High Streets Fund and over £3 million from Greater Manchester's Brownfield Development Fund. The hotel opened in September 2023.

The council's soft-loan table shows £33.662 million owed by Rochdale BTR Ltd on a property loan and £2.045 million in its working-capital borrowing. Rochdale Hotel Holdings Ltd had a £14.270 million property loan and Rochdale Hotel Ltd owed £332,000 in working capital. Together, these total £50.309 million.

The original loan arrangements included payment-holiday periods under which interest accrued and was added to the loans. The council also confirms the lending was provided below market rates in support of its service priorities. That means a growing balance is not, by itself, proof that any company has missed a scheduled payment. The critical missing information is the agreed repayment profile and actual cash returned to the council.

Source: Council draft accounts, printed page 81: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/downloads/file/3217/2025-2026-statement-of-accounts-draft-

Source: Rochdale Development Agency, Upperbanks project details: https://investinrochdale.co.uk/regeneration/projects/upperbanks

THE £2 MILLION INTEREST QUESTION

The 2025/26 loan schedule lists £2.020 million of accrued interest, £159,000 in new advances and £132,000 in repayments. Net contractual loans increased by £2.047 million. The £2.020 million interest recorded is more than fifteen times that year's total repayments.

However, the same page contains an apparent inconsistency. Its narrative says 'no new advances were made', while the adjoining table shows £159,000 of advances to Rochdale BTR Ltd's working-capital loan. The council should reconcile the entries and specify whether the amount was new cash, a transfer or an accounting classification.

The accounts also put the soft loans at a far lower carrying amount, £22.690 million, because below-market loans are discounted for accounting purposes. The council says the concessionary benefit to its subsidiaries is treated as an additional investment; the value of that investment is stated as £27.3 million. The difference is not a £27 million write-off: it reflects accounting treatment of long-term, below-market lending.

WHAT ABOUT THE RISK OF NON-REPAYMENT?

The council's draft accounts record a £472,000 expected-credit-loss allowance across relevant loans at 31 March 2026, of which £267,000 relates to the hotel companies, £189,000 to Rochdale BTR Ltd and £16,000 to other loans. The allowance increased by a net £37,000 during 2025/26. This is a forward-looking credit-risk provision, not proof that a borrower has defaulted or that £472,000 has been lost.

Source: Council draft accounts, printed page 89, impairment table: https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/downloads/file/3217/2025-2026-statement-of-accounts-draft-

ARE THE APARTMENTS AND HOTEL DELIVERING?

According to Rochdale Development Agency's fourth-quarter delivery plan, 155 of the 242 Upperbanks apartments were occupied on 24 March 2026, with eight more reserved. That left 87 unoccupied at the reporting date, although occupancy had improved from earlier in the year. The agency also reported improving hotel occupancy, average room rates and yields. The public report did not supply a complete profit-and-loss or cash-flow analysis establishing whether the companies were meeting their initial business cases.

Source: Rochdale Development Agency 2025/26 Q4 delivery plan: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s122466/2025-26%20RDA%20Delivery%20Plan%20Q4%20FINAL.pdf

WHICH COUNCILLORS WERE INVOLVED — AND WHICH PARTIES?

The scheme's corporate and funding decisions were considered under a Labour-controlled Rochdale Council led by Councillor Neil Emmott (Labour). Councillor John Blundell (Labour and Co-operative) held the Economy and Regeneration portfolio in 2022, when the Upperbanks proposals came before Cabinet. Councillor Carol Wardle (Labour) held the Finance and Corporate portfolio then and continues as the Finance and Growth portfolio holder in 2026.

Councillor Daniel Meredith (Labour and Co-operative), now the Cabinet Member for Regeneration and Housing, has a different documented voting history: minutes of the 22 November 2022 Cabinet meeting state that he expressly requested his vote AGAINST the Upperbanks loan agreement be recorded. The minutes do not specify why he objected, and he must not be portrayed as having approved that agreement.

The 2022 decision approved a loan agreement while delegating the detail of its terms and structure to officers in consultation with relevant portfolio holders. The politicians' portfolios identify responsibility for decisions and oversight, but do not individually establish blame for any loss or wrongdoing.

Source: Rochdale Council, Cabinet meeting of 22 November 2022, item 19: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/ieIssueDetails.aspx?IId=51234&Opt=3&PlanId=0

Source: Rochdale Council, May 2026 Cabinet appointments: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/ieListDocuments.aspx?CId=156&MeetingId=7146

Source: Rochdale Council, Cabinet portfolio responsibilities: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/mgCommitteeDetails.aspx?ID=116

WHY ARE FINANCIAL FORECASTS RESTRICTED?

On 5 February 2026, Cabinet received an Upperbanks trading-company financial update including forecasts compared with the business cases approved in June 2022. The published decision notes that the council is the ultimate parent undertaking and 100% shareholder. But detailed financial enclosures were restricted from public view, leaving the public unable to independently compare the original profitability, occupancy and repayment forecasts with current performance.

Source: Cabinet decision, 5 February 2026: https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/ieDecisionDetails.aspx?AIId=49322

THE COUNCIL TAX COMPARISON — WHAT IT DOES AND DOES NOT SHOW

Roch Valley Radio reported that the £19.5 million figure was a cumulative Council Tax collection shortfall since 2016, drawn from 2024/25 accounts, including about £1.3 million in 2024/25. It is not evidence of a fresh £19.5 million hole in the council's 2026/27 budget, and should not be directly subtracted from or compared with Upperbanks' contractual loan book as though both were immediately available cash.

The comparison does raise a narrower, evidence-based question: how transparent is the council about its own long-term financial commitments, loan repayments and commercial outcomes while it seeks to maximise Council Tax collection?

QUESTIONS REQUIRING ANSWERS

Rochdale Daily is seeking clarity on the contractual repayment timetable, how much loan interest has actually been received in cash, the latest independent valuations of Upperbanks' assets, the trading companies' current profitability, the £159,000 'new advances' discrepancy, and whether a non-confidential comparison with the original 2022 business cases will be released.

Councillor Meredith's recorded vote against the original loan agreement also merits an explanation of his reasons at the time, without assuming those reasons.

Upperbanks has delivered homes and a hotel to the town centre, while published occupancy data show improvement. Neither physical regeneration nor a large outstanding loan balance alone establishes that the scheme has succeeded or failed financially. The public accounts do, however, make a compelling case for clear reporting of when public funds are expected to be repaid and whether the original forecasts are being met.

This investigation is based on the council's DRAFT 2025/26 accounts, which remain subject to audit. Neither the loan balances nor the credit-loss allowances establish unlawful conduct, fraud or improper spending.

Right of reply: Rochdale Borough Council, the named councillors and the Upperbanks companies can send a response, correction or supporting financial evidence to news@rochdaledaily.co.uk.

articles.title: 21 YEARS IN ENGLAND'S BOTTOM 100: Central Rochdale neighbourhood ranked 24th most deprived
articles.excerpt: Government figures show a part of Central Rochdale ranked among England's 100 most deprived neighbourhoods in every index since 2004. Where did regeneration funding go — and what can actually be proved about residents' outcomes?
articles.content_html:
ROCHDALE DAILY INVESTIGATION | 12 OCTOBER 2026

A small part of central Rochdale has been ranked among England's 100 most deprived neighbourhoods in every national assessment since 2004. In the latest official figures it is 24th out of 33,755 areas — and one of just three places in England to have remained in that bottom 100 across all six releases over 21 years.

The finding is not an opposition-party accusation or a campaign slogan. It appears in the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government's English Indices of Deprivation 2025. Its code is E01005482, its statistical name Rochdale 010C, and it falls within the wider Central Rochdale and Mandale Park area.

Official sources: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government, English Indices of Deprivation 2025 statistical release https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025-statistical-release; Government neighbourhood explorer https://deprivation.communities.gov.uk/about-your-neighbourhood/E01005482; Government research report https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025-research-report

2004. 2007. 2010. 2015. 2019. 2025.

The government's researchers identified only three neighbourhoods that were among the 100 most deprived in every one of those six releases: Rochdale 010C, Middlesbrough 003F and Wirral 011C. The government's research report places the Rochdale neighbourhood within the middle-layer area known as Central Rochdale and Mandale Park.

This is not a description of the whole borough and not even of all Central Rochdale. A Lower-layer Super Output Area is a small census-based statistical area, typically home to around 1,500–1,600 people. The boundary of the LSOA matters when discussing local projects and spending. The Department for Education, for example, locates Whitehall Academy on Whitehall Street inside Rochdale 010C, confirming part of the geography, but the area cannot be equated simply with all of Mandale Park or Rochdale town centre.

Source: Department for Education establishment record for Whitehall Academy, LSOA Rochdale 010C https://get-information-schools.service.gov.uk/Establishments/Establishment/Details/151391

WHAT IS ACTUALLY DRIVING THE RANKING?

The 2025 government neighbourhood explorer states that employment deprivation is among the area's most severe problems: fewer than 1% of English neighbourhoods rank as more employment deprived. Rochdale 010C also ranks as the most deprived neighbourhood within the borough for income, with higher-than-usual income deprivation affecting children and older people.

The national index measures seven different types of deprivation: income, employment, education, health, crime, barriers to housing and services, and the living environment. Income and employment carry the largest weights at 22.5% each. In other words, the central issue here is not whether a street looks attractive after regeneration; it is the resources and opportunities available to the people who live there.

Source: Government deprivation explorer https://deprivation.communities.gov.uk/about-your-neighbourhood/E01005482; methodology and domain weights https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025-statistical-release

DOES THIS PROVE THAT ROCHDALE HAS BECOME POORER?

No. The government explicitly warns that deprivation rankings describe RELATIVE circumstances. They do not, on their own, measure absolute changes in poverty, wages, health or household income. Boundaries and methods have changed; the 2025 index includes 55 indicators rather than 39 in 2019. Residents could have experienced improvements while their area's national relative position remained extremely poor.

But staying among the 100 most deprived on six separate occasions is nonetheless compelling evidence of persistent relative disadvantage. A serious assessment of whether interventions worked requires more than a new building or investment headline: longitudinal data on earnings, employment, child poverty, housing quality, health and skills, combined with a clear account of which projects actually reached Rochdale 010C.

Source: Government statistical release and guidance https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025/english-indices-of-deprivation-2025-statistical-release

THE REGENERATION MONEY: BIG HEADLINES, BUT WHICH STREETS?

In a 2023 article, Labour council leader Neil Emmott described a £400 million Rochdale town-centre investment programme, including projects such as Riverside, Upperbanks and the restored Town Hall. The council also says the town secured £23.6 million from the government's Towns Fund, intended to support regeneration, skills and connectivity over a wider geographic area. These are genuine funding and development announcements.

Yet neither £400 million nor £23.6 million is an audited total spent exclusively within Rochdale 010C. The figures include a range of projects, investment types, funding sources and locations. Treating either sum as money spent on the approximately 1,600 residents of this one neighbourhood would be misleading.

Sources: Rochdale Council leader's 2023 regeneration statement https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/council-leaders-blog/investing-future-boroughs-regeneration-continues; council Towns Fund overview https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/business-licensing/towns-fund-money-help-us-improve-rochdale

One more closely relevant entry does appear in Rochdale's formal capital programme: the 2025/26 budget shows £450,000 in external grant funding scheduled for 'Towns Fund – New Homes Central Rochdale', described as land acquisition and remediation before homes are built by Rochdale Boroughwide Housing and private developers. An earlier programme showed £360,000 scheduled in 2023/24 for the similarly named project.

But these are BUDGET entries, not proof that either amount was actually spent. 'Central Rochdale' is also a broader project designation than LSOA Rochdale 010C. The missing link is a project-by-project ledger with actual expenditure, precise sites, housing completions and beneficiary outcomes.

Sources: Rochdale capital programme 2025/26 to 2029/30, 'Towns Fund – New Homes Central Rochdale' https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s112547/Append.%201%20for%20Capital%20Programme%20202526%20to%20202930.pdf; 2023/24 capital programme https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/documents/s94502/Append.%205%20for%20Budget%20Report%20202324.pdf

WHAT HAS BEEN DONE ABOUT POVERTY?

The council approved 'The Future We Deserve', its borough-wide 2024–2029 anti-poverty strategy, in March 2024. The authority described rising destitution and inequality as reasons for taking a long-term approach. From April 2026 it also began allocating around £5 million in government-backed Crisis and Resilience Fund support across the borough to assist residents facing emergencies, housing pressures and the cost of essentials.

Those programmes matter. They are also different in purpose from capital investment: emergency food and housing support can reduce immediate hardship, while regeneration may seek longer-term jobs and productivity. Neither a borough-wide budget nor a policy document establishes how many residents of Rochdale 010C received support or whether the area's underlying deprivation indicators improved.

Sources: March 2024 Cabinet decision approving anti-poverty strategy https://rochdale.moderngov.co.uk/ieIssueDetails.aspx?IId=55806&Opt=3; council Crisis and Resilience Fund https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/cost-living/crisis-resilience-fund

THE COUNCIL'S OWN RESPONSE TO SOCIAL MOBILITY CONCERNS

In a 2025 response to a social-mobility investigation, Rochdale Council acknowledged significant poverty, deprivation and inequality while pointing to improvements in town centres, education, employment opportunities and transport. It highlighted Rochdale Sixth Form College, Hopwood Hall College, the restored Town Hall and wider development proposals as assets that could improve opportunity.

These represent reasonable arguments for regeneration. But they are evidence of provision and investment, not by themselves proof that low-income residents in Rochdale 010C have entered stable, well-paid work or escaped hardship. This investigation has not obtained an LSOA-specific outcomes evaluation to test that claim.

Source: Rochdale Borough Council response to the Independent Commission on Social Mobility, 2025 https://socialmobility.independent-commission.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Rochdale-Borough-Council-response-to-Deep-dives_-a-local-perspective-on-social-mobility.docx.pdf

WHO SHOULD ANSWER?

Rochdale Council is Labour-controlled, led by Councillor Neil Emmott. The Central Rochdale ward is represented in October 2026 by Councillor Farooq Ahmed (Workers Party of Britain), Councillor Waqar Khan (Workers Party of Britain) and Councillor Sameena Zaheer (Labour and Co-operative), who also holds a Cabinet portfolio for Corporate, Governance and Transformation. The ward is a different boundary from the statistical neighbourhood and its current councillors did not all serve throughout the 21-year period.

These affiliations identify democratic responsibility and representation; the deprivation index does not establish misconduct, negligence or causation by any individual councillor or political party.

Sources: Council councillor directory https://democracy.rochdale.gov.uk/mgUserInfo.aspx?UID=7214; https://democracy.rochdale.gov.uk/mgUserInfo.aspx?UID=5385; Workers Party councillor directory https://www.workerspartygb.org/our_councillors; council control https://www.rochdale.gov.uk/councilmeetings

SEVEN QUESTIONS THAT DESERVE DOCUMENTED ANSWERS

1. Which completed, current and planned projects since 2004 have physically overlapped the boundary of LSOA E01005482?

2. For each project, how much public funding was approved, contracted and actually spent — separated from private investment and borough-wide allocations?

3. What proportion of jobs created or safeguarded under those programmes went to residents of this exact neighbourhood, and at what wages?

4. How have child income deprivation, employment deprivation, housing conditions and school attendance changed in absolute terms over time, not merely national rankings?

5. What specific measurable targets did the 2024–2029 Anti-Poverty Strategy set for the most deprived neighbourhoods, and how does Rochdale 010C perform against them?

6. What data will the council use to demonstrate that forthcoming developments are benefiting the people already living in this neighbourhood, rather than simply changing the appearance or population mix of nearby streets?

7. Will the council publish an independently auditable, geographically itemised account of 20 years of spending and outcomes, and allow residents to examine the results?

WHY IT MATTERS

Rochdale's new shops, college provision, housing developments, town-hall restoration and cultural attractions are visible and can produce genuine benefits. The government's latest deprivation statistics show a different and equally important side of local economic life: one neighbourhood has remained among England's most deprived in every national index for more than two decades.

That is not proof that £400 million was wasted. It is proof that the success of regeneration cannot be established from the value of construction projects alone. The ultimate test is whether residents gain lasting opportunities, better homes, improved health and higher disposable incomes.

Rochdale Daily is inviting the council, its regeneration agency, the ward councillors, relevant public bodies and local community organisations to provide a full geographic spending-and-outcomes breakdown and their responses to these findings. Corrections and right of reply can be sent to news@rochdaledaily.co.uk.

articles.title: Spudbros Opens New Location at EG Station on Manchester Road in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Jacket potato fans in Rochdale welcomed the opening of Spudbros at EG Station on Manchester Road, with the first 100 customers receiving a free meal.
articles.content_html:
Spudbros, a popular jacket potato brand from Preston, has officially opened its new location at the EG Station on Manchester Road in Rochdale. The opening attracted large crowds, with many eager customers queuing for the chance to try the viral spud offerings.

The first 100 customers through the doors received a free meal, further adding to the excitement of the launch. This new outlet is expected to bring a fresh dining option to the area, catering to both locals and visitors alike.

Spudbros is known for its variety of toppings and quick service, making it a popular choice for those looking for a quick bite. The opening at EG Station marks a significant expansion for the brand, which has gained a loyal following since its inception.

Local residents can now enjoy the convenience of having Spudbros nearby, potentially boosting foot traffic in the area. The new location is likely to become a go-to spot for jacket potato enthusiasts in Rochdale.

articles.title: Hollingworth Lake to host Wave of Light walk remembering babies and children
articles.excerpt: Families affected by baby or child loss are invited to meet at Hollingworth Lake's beach at 6.30pm on Thursday 15 October for a remembrance walk and 7pm candle-lighting, with bereavement charities and helplines available for support.
articles.content_html:
Families and friends affected by the death of a baby or child are invited to gather at Hollingworth Lake in Littleborough on Thursday 15 October for a candlelit remembrance walk at the end of Baby Loss Awareness Week.

The community invitation asks people to meet at the beach at Hollingworth Lake at 6.30pm. The group plans to walk together around the lake, pausing approximately halfway round at a scenic point to light candles at 7pm as part of the worldwide Wave of Light.

The invitation is open to anyone who has experienced miscarriage, stillbirth, neonatal death, the death of a baby or the loss of a child at any age, as well as relatives, friends, neighbours and others wishing to show their support.

One of the people behind the gathering said that every year they light a candle for the babies they remember. This year, rather than marking the occasion alone, they hope people can come together for a shared moment of remembrance.

Baby Loss Awareness Week takes place each year from 9 to 15 October. At 7pm on 15 October, families around the world take part in the Wave of Light by lighting candles in memory of babies who have died. The Hollingworth Lake walk extends a welcome to those remembering children of all ages.

Those attending can bring a candle or battery-operated light, dress warmly for an October evening and carry a torch for the walk. Please keep a safe distance from the water, take care on paths after dark, never leave flames unattended, and take all candles and materials home rather than leaving them by or in the lake. Details of accessibility arrangements have not been provided in the original invitation.

EVENT DETAILS: Thursday 15 October 2026. Meet at 6.30pm at the beach at Hollingworth Lake, Littleborough, Rochdale, OL15 0AQ. Walk together and stop to light candles at 7pm. This article reports a community invitation; the charities listed below are support resources and are not described as organisers or sponsors of the event.

WHERE TO FIND HELP AFTER BABY OR CHILD LOSS

Grief can affect parents, partners, siblings, grandparents and friends, sometimes long after the death. No one has to attend the walk or speak about a loss to deserve support. The following verified organisations offer specialist information, listening services and, in some cases, counselling or local peer groups.

Sands — confidential help for anyone affected by pregnancy or baby loss, including bereaved relatives and friends. Free national helpline: 0808 164 3332; email: helpline@sands.org.uk; website: https://www.sands.org.uk/support-you/how-we-offer-support/helpline. Telephone hours are Monday to Friday 10am–3pm and Tuesday to Thursday 6pm–9pm, excluding bank holidays.

Child Bereavement UK — support for parents and carers when a baby or child dies, and for bereaved children and young people. Free helpline: 0800 02 888 40, Monday to Friday 8am–8pm, excluding bank holidays. Text or WhatsApp: 07418 341 800 (WhatsApp support for ages 13 and over). Website: https://www.childbereavementuk.org/.

Finding Rainbows — Greater Manchester peer support for families affected by early pregnancy loss or the death of a baby or child. Email: finding.rainbows@outlook.com; website: https://www.findingrainbows.org/.

Tommy's — specialist midwife-led advice on miscarriage, stillbirth, pregnancy after loss and pregnancy-related wellbeing. Free helpline: 0800 0147 800, Monday to Friday 9am–5pm. Email: midwife@tommys.org; website: https://www.tommys.org/. This is a non-urgent advice line.

The Lullaby Trust — specialist bereavement support after the sudden and unexpected death of a baby or young child. Free helpline: 0808 802 6868; website: https://www.lullabytrust.org.uk/bereavement-support/find-support/. Phone support is available Monday to Friday 10am–2pm and weekends and public holidays 6pm–10pm.

Antenatal Results and Choices (ARC) — confidential, non-directive support after difficult antenatal test results, fetal diagnosis and pregnancy loss following a decision to end a pregnancy for medical reasons. Helpline: 020 7713 7486, Monday to Friday 10am–5.30pm. Text: 07908 683004; email: info@arc-uk.org; website: https://www.arc-uk.org/.

Miscarriage Association — information and support for anyone affected by miscarriage, ectopic pregnancy or molar pregnancy. Website: https://www.miscarriageassociation.org.uk/.

Petals — specialist counselling for people affected by pregnancy loss, stillbirth or neonatal death, subject to service eligibility and referral arrangements. Website: https://www.petalscharity.org/.

4Louis — bereavement support resources and memory boxes for families following the death of a baby or child. Website: https://www.4louis.co.uk/.

SUDC UK — information, bereavement support and research relating to sudden unexplained death in childhood. Contact: 07880 350942, Monday to Thursday 9am–5pm; email: info@sudc.org.uk; website: https://sudc.org.uk/.

Greater Manchester NHS PETALS Perinatal Trauma and Loss Service — assessment and therapeutic support for people experiencing trauma related to birth, pregnancy or baby loss. A healthcare professional can make a referral. Telephone: 0161 271 0188 (option 4), Monday to Friday 9am–5pm; website: https://www.gmmh.nhs.uk/petals.

If you need somebody to talk to now, Samaritans offers free emotional support day and night on 116 123 (https://www.samaritans.org/). For urgent mental health support in England, contact NHS 111 and select the mental health option. Call 999 if someone is in immediate danger.

articles.excerpt: Canine Country Club has introduced new puppy sessions and enrichment classes following a successful animal activities licence inspection, enhancing its services for local dog owners.
articles.content_html:

The new puppy programmes will be held on Thursdays from 10am to noon, providing a structured environment for young dogs to learn and socialise. In addition to these sessions, the club will offer one-to-one enrichment classes designed for dogs that may be timid, less social, or older, allowing them to engage in activities in a quieter setting.

Stefanie emphasised that the welfare of the dogs is her top priority, stating, "Providing a welfare-focused program that prioritises the dogs' best interests has always been my top priority." This initiative aims to cater to the diverse needs of dogs in the community, ensuring they receive the attention and care they require.

Local dog owners interested in these new classes can contact Canine Country Club for further information and to book their spots. The introduction of these classes is expected to enhance the services available to pet owners in Rochdale, providing valuable opportunities for socialisation and enrichment for their dogs.

articles.title: Rochdale October half-term 2026: school dates and free family activities
articles.excerpt: The council's recommended half-term runs from 26 to 30 October. Here are verified free activities at Rochdale Town Hall, Wardle Library and local family hubs, plus what parents should check before travelling.
articles.content_html:
Families across Rochdale, Heywood, Middleton, Littleborough and Milnrow can start planning the October school break, with the council recommending Monday 26 to Friday 30 October 2026 as the autumn half-term holiday. The dates are a borough-wide recommended pattern, rather than a guarantee for every school, so parents should check their own school's calendar before booking childcare or a trip.

One of the clearest free options announced so far is at Rochdale Town Hall. Its Spooktacular Half Term programme is advertised for every day from Monday 26 October to Sunday 1 November, running from 10am to 4pm at the Town Hall on The Esplanade, OL16 1AZ. The organiser describes family-friendly Halloween activities, with free entry and no advance booking required. More detailed individual activities have not yet all been listed, so it is worth checking the official Town Hall event information before travelling.

For families wanting a short outing at the end of the break, Wardle Library's Kids' Club is listed in the council's October events calendar for Saturday 31 October. The free session runs from 10am until 12.30pm at 448 Birch Road, Wardle, OL12 9LH. It is aimed at families with children aged four and over and normally includes crafts, activities and challenges. The council says there is no need to book.

Parents and carers with younger children also have the borough's family hubs to investigate. Council information lists activities for children aged up to five at locations including Heybrook, Howard Street, Meanwood, Castleton, Deeplish and Sandbrook, as well as centres in Middleton, Heywood, Littleborough and the wider Pennines area. The council describes these activities as free unless otherwise stated. The listing is a directory rather than a confirmed half-term timetable, so families should consult their nearest hub's current programme instead of assuming ordinary weekly sessions continue during the holiday.

Not every regular children's library session runs during school holidays. Some Bookstart activities are explicitly described as term-time sessions, making it especially important to check dates rather than turn up on the strength of a weekly listing.

Parents trying to keep costs down can therefore rely on the confirmed free Town Hall programme and check the Wardle Library listing, while using the council's event directory to see whether anything else is added nearer the time. This guide covers confirmed information available on 13 October; opening arrangements and individual sessions may change.

Passengers are advised to plan their journeys ahead of time and can contact the Metrolink customer service for assistance, especially as the lift at Besses o' th' Barn tram stop is out of service. articles.title: Rochdale’s takeaway winning streak continues as Tandoori Flames takes North West title
articles.excerpt: Littleborough’s Tandoori Flames is the latest Rochdale borough business to take a regional ARTA title, following wins for River Beal in Milnrow and Wild Ginger in Littleborough last year.
articles.content_html:
First Milnrow, now Littleborough. The North West Takeaway of the Year award has found its way to Rochdale borough for the second year running.

Tandoori Flames, on Church Street in Littleborough, won the regional title at the Asian Restaurant and Takeaway Awards (ARTA), held at the London Hilton on Park Lane on Monday 12 October.

Last year's winner was River Beal Indian Takeaway in Milnrow. And that was not the borough's only success in 2025. Wild Ginger Restaurant in Littleborough also took the North West Restaurant of the Year award.

Three regional awards in two years, all earned by businesses in Littleborough and Milnrow. Not a bad record for the local curry scene.

The 2026 competition attracted more than 1,250 nominations from across the UK. Tandoori Flames and River Beal both appeared on the North West's ten strong takeaway shortlist, alongside businesses from Bolton, Manchester, Wigan and other parts of the region.

Tandoori Flames emerged with the title. The organisers say their judging process considered customer nominations, online reviews, food hygiene ratings and assessments by a panel of judges. That matters because the award is not based on a single enthusiastic recommendation, or merely on how many people happen to vote.

The Littleborough win continues a striking run for neighbouring communities in the borough. River Beal's 2025 title showed that a Milnrow takeaway could compete for regional honours. Wild Ginger's restaurant award in the same year gave Littleborough a victory of its own. Tandoori Flames has now brought another takeaway trophy back to the area.

The ceremony, hosted by presenter Samantha Simmonds and comedian Paul Sinha, brought together restaurateurs and hospitality professionals from around the country. Rochdale MP Paul Waugh was among the guests.

ARTA founder Mohammed Munim congratulated the winners and finalists and drew attention to the rising costs facing independent restaurants. Food, energy and staffing bills have all placed pressure on hospitality businesses, even where customer demand remains strong.

An award does not tell us everything about a restaurant or takeaway. Prices, consistency, service and personal taste still matter to customers. But these results provide a useful measure of how Rochdale businesses are performing beyond the borough.

And there is something pleasing about where the trophies have ended up. The awards cover a region with far larger centres of population and long established dining destinations. Yet, for two years, the takeaway title has gone to addresses in Milnrow and Littleborough.

Rochdale Daily congratulates Tandoori Flames on its 2026 win and recognises the achievements of River Beal and Wild Ginger in 2025.

Have you eaten at any of the three? Tell us what you rate on the menu in the comments. We are always interested in a good local recommendation.

articles.title: Rochdale Sixth Form College Students Disciplined for Ranking Looks in Online Group
articles.excerpt: Students at Rochdale Sixth Form College have faced disciplinary action after creating a Microsoft Teams group that instructed members to categorise themselves based on physical attractiveness, with rules enforced by a self-styled 'Founding Father'.
articles.content_html:
Students at Rochdale Sixth Form College have been disciplined following the establishment of a Microsoft Teams group where members were instructed to rank themselves by physical attractiveness. The group, named 'Rochdale Sixth Form College BP Club', used terminology associated with online incel and manosphere communities, with 'BP' standing for black pill.

The organiser of the group, who referred to himself as the 'Founding Father', mandated that members categorise themselves into labels such as 'Chad', 'HTN', and 'LTN', which ranked individuals from exceptionally attractive to below average. The organiser warned of 'serious consequences' for those who did not adhere to the group's rules and demanded the use of 'formal language' in communications.

Messages shared within the group included derogatory comments about other students and profanity, as well as a target to expand the group to 100 members by the following week. The organiser also issued strikes to members who failed to comply with the established rules, further enforcing a culture of ranking based on looks.

The disciplinary actions taken by the college highlight the institution's stance against such behaviour, which is seen as detrimental to student wellbeing and inclusivity. The college has not disclosed specific details regarding the nature of the disciplinary measures imposed.

We want to bring you unfiltered reporting — stories that celebrate our communities, champion our businesses, ask difficult questions and hold public institutions to account without telling readers what they should think.

Eighty-six thousand readers in a month means something to us because behind every number is a person: a parent checking what is happening at school, a resident following a council decision, a family looking for something to do, a small business hoping to be noticed or a neighbour who simply wants to understand the place they call home.

We want you to know that we read every email. We value your tips, your corrections, your concerns and your encouragement. Some of the stories that matter most begin when one resident takes the time to get in touch.

And we have a big ambition for what comes next: to reach 200,000 readers by November. It is an ambitious target, not a forecast, but we want more people across Rochdale, Heywood, Middleton, Littleborough, Milnrow and the wider borough to know that their local stories have a home here.

If you have enjoyed an article, please leave a comment. If you disagree, tell us why. If something important is happening in your street or community, get in touch. Follow the Rochdale Daily Facebook page and share our articles with friends, family and neighbours.

Your comments, questions and suggestions help shape what we investigate and where we direct our attention. We won't always get everything right, and when we don't, we want to hear about it, correct mistakes and do better.

We do not want this to be a newspaper that talks at Rochdale. We want it to be a newspaper that listens to Rochdale.

To all 86,000 of you: thank you for putting your trust in us. We intend to work to earn it every day.

Please comment, follow, share and stay with us. This is your newspaper. We want to work for you — and for our town.

articles.title: Queues form from 7.20am as SpudBros Express opens in Rochdale
articles.excerpt: Early customers queued from around 7.20am for the new SpudBros Express outlet on Manchester New Road, with the first 100 customers promised a free loaded jacket potato at its midday launch.
articles.content_html:
Jacket potato fans were reported to be queuing from as early as 7.20am on Tuesday 13 October as SpudBros Express prepared to open its new Rochdale outlet.

The takeaway concession, at Manchester New Road, Rochdale, OL11 3PT, officially launched at midday with a promotion offering a free jacket potato to the first 100 customers through the doors. The reported 7.20am start would put some early arrivals more than four and a half hours ahead of opening.

Rochdale Daily received a report of large queues forming early in the morning. The precise number of people waiting has not been independently verified.

The Preston-founded SpudBros brand has built an enormous following online with videos of generously topped jacket potatoes. Its Express arm is expanding beyond traditional high streets through a partnership with food business Taster and forecourt operator EG On The Move.

The menu includes the Tram Classic, with garlic butter, a three-cheese mix, baked beans, crispy onions and Tram Sauce, alongside the Spudfather with chilli con carne, other loaded options and build-your-own potatoes.

The Rochdale concession is part of a wider plan to bring SpudBros Express to 30 EG On The Move roadside sites over three years. In an opening announcement, SpudBros co-founder Jacob Nelson said the Greater Manchester launch felt particularly special given the business's Preston roots.

According to the launch announcement, the new Rochdale outlet is expected to open seven days a week: 11am to 9pm from Sunday to Thursday and 11am to 10pm on Fridays and Saturdays. Opening-day trading began at noon.

More information about the menu and locations is available at the official SpudBros Express website, www.spudbrosexpress.com.
